fact_en:
Why are racing cars built so wide and low?

They're built that way to keep their center of gravity super low! This stops the car from rolling over when zooming around corners at high speed.
fact_bis:
Ngano nga lapad ug ubos ang mga racing car?

Gilaraw sila aron ubos kaayo ang center of gravity! Dili kini maluod kon mo-ligo sa mga kurba sa taas nga bilis.

findings.note: The card's payoff — a low centre of gravity stops the car ROLLING OVER when cornering — is destroyed: "Dili kini maluod kon mo-ligo sa mga kurba sa taas nga bilis." maluod = to feel NAUSEATED/queasy (roll over = maligid/matumba), and mo-ligo = to TAKE A BATH (turn a corner = moliko). Reads as "it won't get nauseous when it bathes in the curves." Nothing else in the card states the rollover fact.

fact_en:
What is rolling resistance, and why do underinflated tires use more fuel?

Rolling resistance is the friction force between a tire and the road! Underinflated tires have higher rolling resistance, causing greater fuel consumption.
fact_bis:
Unsa ang rolling resistance, ug nganong mas daghang gasolina ang gulong nga kulang sa hangin?

Ang rolling resistance mao ang kiskisan sa gulong ug daan! Ang gulong nga kulang sa hangin adunay mas taas nga rolling resistance, nagdugang sa gasolina.

findings.note: Definition sentence: 'Ang rolling resistance mao ang kiskisan sa gulong ug daan!' — Tagalog false friend: daan = road in Tagalog, but in Cebuano daan = OLD (road is dalan). The card's core definition (friction between tyre and road) becomes 'friction of the tyre and the old', and no other sentence names the road, so a child cannot recover what the tyre rubs against. Same slip recurs in ffct-24842 ('shock sa daan'), where the rest of the sentence still carries the fact.

fact_en: A ship floats because the water it pushes away weighs exactly the same as the ship! Engineers design the hull shape to keep this Archimedean balance.
fact_bis: Naglutaw ang barko tungod kay ang tubig nga gipalit niini katumbas sa tibuok timbang niini! Gilaraw sa mga engineer ang hull shape aron masiguro kining Archimedean balance.

findings.note: Buoyancy card: 'ang tubig nga gipalit niini katumbas sa tibuok timbang niini'. In Cebuano gipalit = BOUGHT (palit = to buy; the Tagalog sense 'exchanged/displaced' does not exist in Cebuano). The child reads 'the water the ship BOUGHT weighs the same as the ship' — the displacement idea, which is the whole fact of the card, is never stated anywhere else on the card and cannot be recovered. Corpus-wide gipalit is used only for buying (bought bananas, bought salt, bought fuel).

fact_en:
Why does a sharp nail easily pierce wood or a wall?

The sharp tip concentrates force into a very tiny area, creating very high pressure that drives the nail in!
fact_bis:
Nganong sayon mosulod ang matalas nga pako sa kahoy o dingding?

Nagtipon ang matalas nga tumoy sa puwersa ngadto sa napakagamay nga lawak, naghimo og napakataas nga presyon nga nagmaneho sa pako!

findings.note: Title 'Tulos sa Matalas nga Pako' plus both body uses: 'sayon mosulod ang matalas nga pako sa kahoy' / 'presyon nga nagmaneho sa pako'. In Cebuano pako = WING (or fern); a nail is lansang. Nothing on the card restores 'nail' — the headline and the answer both describe a sharp WING being driven into wood. Corpus-wide this batch's own sibling cards use lansang for nail and pako only for wings (kabog, buyog, insekto).

fact_en: Sharp things like nails and knives are dangerous because their tiny tips squeeze all the force into a small area, creating huge pressure that pierces skin easily!
fact_bis: Delikado ang mga matalas nga butang sama sa pako ug kutsilyo tungod kay ang gamay nga tumoy nagpugos sa tanan nga puwersa sa gamay nga lugar, naghimo og dako nga presyon nga dali nga mosulod sa panit!

findings.note: Body: "Delikado ang mga matalas nga butang sama sa PAKO ug kutsilyo" for EN "nails and knives". In Cebuano pako = WING (or fern); a nail is lansang. The card is about tiny tips concentrating force to pierce skin, so the exemplar object is load-bearing, and nothing in the card (title "Mahait nga Butang", terms, body) ever restores "nail" — the child is told wings are sharp and dangerous. The terms field carries the same bad pair ("nail,pako").

fact_en:
How did ancient people move giant stones without machines?

They used long sticks as levers to lift heavy stones! This is one of our earliest technologies, way before the written word.
fact_bis:
Unsaon pagbalhin sa mga karaan nga tawo og dagkong bato nga walay makina?

Naggamit sila og taas nga mga kawayan isip lever aron ibangon ang mabug-at nga bato! Kini usa sa pinakamaagang teknolohiya sa wala pa ang pagsulat.

findings.note: title_bis "Karaang Lebre" for title_en "Ancient Levers". lebre (< Sp. liebre) = a HARE in Cebuano; a lever is palanka/pangbangon, not lebre. The headline a child sees therefore announces "ancient hare" over a simple-machines card; the body only uses the English word "lever", so the Cebuano label is never corrected in Cebuano.

fact_en: Caught outside in a lightning storm? Crouch low with feet together, head tucked between your knees. Don't lie flat! This makes you a smaller target and keeps you safer.
fact_bis: Naabtan ka sa gawas samtang may kidlat? Paglubo nga ubos, duhaon ang mga tiil, itago ang ulo sa tuhod. Ayaw paghigda! Mas gamay ang target nimo ug mas luwas ka.

findings.note: title_bis "Lukso Gagmay Target Kidlat" — "lukso" is JUMP in Cebuano (cf. ffct-25232 in this same batch: "mga batang naglukso" = jumping kids), but the card is "Crouch Low in Lightning". The headline tells a child to JUMP during a lightning storm, the opposite of the safety action. The body does not restore a crouch verb either: "Paglubo nga ubos" is not a recognisable Cebuano word for crouch (pungko/duko) and "duhaon ang mga tiil" garbles "feet together"; only "Ayaw paghigda" and "itago ang ulo sa tuhod" survive, so the instructed posture is not recoverable from the Cebuano alone.

fact_en: The eardrum is a thin membrane inside your ear. When sound waves hit it, it vibrates just like the skin of a real drum!
fact_bis: Ang eardrum usa ka manipis nga lamad sa sulod sa imong tainga. Kung matahasan sa mga sound wave, nalingkod kini sama sa panit sa tinuod nga tambol!

findings.note: Eardrum. "Kung matahasan sa mga sound wave, NALINGKOD kini sama sa panit sa tinuod nga tambol" — 'it sits like the skin of a real drum'. The single fact the card exists to teach (the eardrum vibrates when sound hits it) is gone; the card never says mokurog/vibrate.

fact_en: The cochlea is a spiral organ in the inner ear with tiny hair cells. When they vibrate, they send electrical signals to the brain as sound!
fact_bis: Ang cochlea usa ka spiral nga organ sa inner ear nga adunay gagmayng hair cells. Kung nagalingkod sila, nagapadala sila og electrical signals sa utok ingon tunog!

findings.note: Cochlea. "Kung NAGALINGKOD sila, nagapadala sila og electrical signals sa utok" — 'when they sit'. The trigger for the hair cells firing (vibration) is replaced by sitting, and vibration appears nowhere else in the Cebuano, so the conversion mechanism is lost.

fact_en: Your inner ear has three semicircular canals filled with fluid! When the fluid moves, it tells your brain which way you're turning to keep your balance.
fact_bis: Ang imong inner ear adunay tulo ka semicircular canals nga puno sa likido! Kung molihok ang likido, nagisulti kini sa utok kung asa ka nagikod aron mabalanse ka.

findings.note: title_bis "Canals sa BALI" for title_en 'Semicircular Balance Canals'. bali = BROKEN/fracture (or to flip over) in Cebuano; balance is balanse/timbang. The body has it right ('aron mabalanse ka'), so the title is the outlier and reads as 'canals of the broken'.

fact_en:
Why do the bigger gongs in a kulintang make a deeper sound?

The kulintang is a set of small gongs from Mindanao! The larger gongs give a lower pitch simply because they vibrate more slowly.
fact_bis:
Nganong ang mas dagkong gong sa kulintang nagahatag og mas ubos nga tunog?

Ang kulintang usa ka grupo sa gagmayng gong gikan sa Mindanao! Ang mas dagkong gong nagahatag og mas ubos nga pitch tungod kay nagalingkod nga mas hinay.

findings.note: Kulintang gongs. "...mas ubos nga pitch tungod kay NAGALINGKOD nga mas hinay" — the causal clause that answers the headline question ('because they vibrate more slowly') becomes 'because they sit more slowly'. No other vibration word in the card, so the reason is unrecoverable.

fact_en:
How does a simple bamboo flute actually make music?

A bamboo flute makes sound when the air column inside the tube vibrates! The exact length of this vibrating air column is what determines the pitch.
fact_bis:
Unsaon paghimo og tunog ang simpleng bamboo flute?

Nagahimo og tunog ang bamboo flute kung nagalingkod ang hangin sa sulod sa tubo! Ang gitas-on sa nagalingkod nga air column maoy nagtino sa pitch.

findings.note: Bamboo flute. "kung NAGALINGKOD ang hangin sa sulod sa tubo... ang gitas-on sa NAGALINGKOD nga air column" — lingkod = TO SIT, not to vibrate (mokurog / mag-vibrate). The card's whole mechanism (the air column vibrates) is replaced by 'the air sits inside the tube'; nothing else in the card mentions vibration, and emph_bis even highlights the broken phrase. A child gets no mechanism at all. Corpus's own correct words appear in other cards (mokurog in ffct-25334/25335, nag-vibrate in ffct-25392/25395/25398).
